comments.author: dmos62
comments.text:
What are peoples' takes on why LLMs struggle to write things in a human-readable way? I've watched Astra and the like write PR descriptions that are middle-school level: as if it struggles to distinguish what it knows (having read the code, having done the debugging) and what someone who hasn't read the code and hasn't participated in the debugging (his target audience) knows. It'll make references to parts of the solution, or of the problem being solved, without contextualizing it, making the references useless, serving only to add confusion to the text.
Terence Tao's take was that LLMs don't understand what is trivial (in a proof, for example) and what is interesting and novel: it gives everything equal weight, or, in Tao's paraphrased words, the LLM will talk at length about something trivial and then write only a single sentence about something novel.
I wonder what peoples' intuition about this is.

comments.author: liendolucas
comments.text:
I personally think that the mistake here is to have been forced to publish. While the result of this proof (if correct) would be groundbraking I believe the true value is in understanding!
The computer can definitely say "yes" or "no" pretty much like an oracle could say it but 17m lines of Lean code tells absolutely nothing to the math community. Who's going to put effort to work on that? What progress does that bring to mathematics?
In contrast the attempted proof is "only" 940 pages that can be digested by human beings and I believe that's exactly the point of it. Even if incorrect perhaps there are many innovative techniques that can still applied elsewhere.
If I was Masullo I wouldn't have published anything because I would think that the work was still safe and with plenty of time to keep working on it.

comments.author: shank-false-rin
comments.text:
I'm not really sure if AI should be compared to regular tools (abacuses, calculators, ...).
If a dictator of some random country rounded up a group of mathematicians and ordered them to churn out every possible way to prove the RH, and those mathematicians eventually succeeded, would we say the dictator proved the RH thanks to the dictator's unique visionary insight in assigning the mathematicians that task?
This should be the bar: did the machine just help you do something faster in the same way that you could very realistically have done yourself? Like, could you have written the 17 million lines of Lean if you wanted to?

Are mathematicians completely nuts? Is this high school? This guy has proven RH without any AI assistance, maybe modulo a few minor adjustments. Who gives a crap if Alpöge was first™ by a few hours? Give them both credit and the Fields medal.
Mathematicians go on and on about how we have to limit AI companies' doings so as to not disrupt their social structure. If so, then they should act like adults. comments.author: dead_hn_theory
comments.text:
My only issue with using AI for these things is that the "brute force" method yields very little new insight. I don't want to say the final answer is irrelevant, I'm sure it has uses (even though in some cases mathematicians make assumptions for their own work).
The
new insight
that I am referring to is that mathematicians on their way to prove one thing sometimes end up having to invent new ways of looking at problems which not only leads to a re-evaluation of existing solutions for other problems, and hence potentially a simplification of a proof using new ways of seeing, but they also open up vast fields that others can then study and apply in a multitude of unforeseen ways. Brute force is highly unlikely to have any of this, and I'd say this is more important than the proof because they themselves are never quite "finished" due to these discoveries.
(To be a bit more dour about things: The GRH is so darn important that we've learned
absolutely nothing
from this solution.)

stories.title_en: Perplexity and Intelligence

comments.author: hazrmard
comments.text:
Perplexity is not defined in the article. FYI:
Perplexity is the degree of surprise the model has in predicting the next token, over a sequence of tokens. At the worst case, perplexity is equal to the size of the vocabulary. At the best case, perplexity is 1.
So, given a sequence of tokens, "e = m c ^ 2", if the p(token | prev tokens) = 1 for every token, perplexity ends up being 1. If, however, it's a random predictor, the p(token | prev tokens) is 1/vocab for every token, and perplexity ends up being len(vocab).
The article plots log(perplexity) on the y-axis, which puts the best case at 0 (i.e. log 1).

comments.author: jrflo
comments.text:
This trend is pretty shocking to me. I assumed that we had moved beyond cross-entropy loss being important with the increasing use of RL, it's wild that the trend is so clear. Really nice to have such a simple benchmark instead of the increasingly convoluted ones that are getting spun up every day.
Also, I wonder what happened with GPT 4.5? I think o1 was the start of true reasoning models, right? I was using Claude at the time so I can't remember.

comments.author: d_burfoot
comments.text:
The perplexity / intelligence correspondence is one of those ideas that is surprising at first, but in retrospect could not work any other way. The "magic" of intelligence is the ability to extract sophisticated world models from large volumes of raw sensor data. The prediction (=compression) rate on the raw data stream is exactly the metric that captures this progress.
I argued this point in a 2008 paper:
https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-69134-1_...
I elaborated on this idea in my 2011 book:
https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.5466
I used the word "reusability" to express the idea that the world models obtained via the large scale data compression task could be repurposed for other tasks.
(So, Burfoot, if you were so prescient, why aren't you a rich and famous frontier lab researcher? The answer is: I did not think neural nets would scale up).

comments.author: reasonableklout
comments.text:
Microsoft is now signing on to this effort to measure and potentially limit their base model perplexities, see this tweet from Mustafa Suleyman adding the MAI models to the chart:
https://x.com/mustafasuleyman/status/2124663594449318173
>
We're committed to sharing our pre-training progress on a common held-out evaluation set. With OpenAI's permission, we report MAI-2 Base on their evaluation set. Its log-perplexity is 0.819, putting it in the same ballpark as the GPT-5.6 Sol base model. Our model uses the same tokenizer as OpenAI, so the numbers are directly comparable.
>
In the future, to be able to compare across labs we might need to report bits-per-byte (BPB) rather than perplexity since different labs use different tokenizers. We will also need different evaluation datasets - the fact we have access to OpenAI's evaluation dataset is a special case.

comments.author: tensor
comments.text:
I'm a bit skeptical about the claim that particular abilities "emerge" at given perplexities. For instance, there are smaller models that are specifically trained on math, and I imagine those models have much higher general perplexity on other tasks.
On the other hand,
assuming you have appropriate training data for a task
, then yes obviously perplexity is going to measure performance on that task. Being able to predict the next task token is obviously going to be a near perfect correlation with accuracy on the task.

comments.author: ACCount39
comments.text:
Interesting that GPT-4.5 is the only discontinuity on the graph.
The oversized monster LLM has performed worse than CoT-trained o1 and o3 on the benchmarks, so CoT + RL clearly provided better "real world performance" improvements - let alone "price/performance."
But if pre-training perplexity on held-out data really does measure something like "base model IQ" or "base model g factor", then it does support the hypothesis that 4.5 still had more "intellectual potential" than the o-series.
So, if you were wondering why do AI companies train 10T+ monsters now, and are taking aim at 100T too? It's because scale works.

comments.author: theptip
comments.text:
> I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors).
Very positive to see this proposed from OpenAI. I hope Anthropic and GDM follow suit.
I suspect it’s not sufficient, but definitely necessary.
The one concern I have is if we pin pretraining perplexity, then there will be more pressure on RL for progress.
It seems that pre-training actually led to fairly human-aligned models; the Overton window is in some sense latent in the corpus.
On the other hand, heavily RL’d models exhibit more reward seeking behavior, and seem to be decoupling from the friendly assistant persona in certain contexts. And swarm RL (as OpenAI is doing) produces agents with quite inhuman tendencies to self-sacrifice for other instances (see Hugging Face).
So, I hope we also pair this with some measure of alignment or pacing for RL, too.

stories.title_en: Assume People Are Not Interested in Your Blog Post

comments.author: Agentlien
comments.text:
> If you do not write for other people, stop reading this now.
This is the opening line. But in my view this is part of what defines a blog. You write for yourself and share hoping others will enjoy it, as well.
An overwhelming part of the time I feel the post title and opening paragraph tells me whether a piece is for me, without the author having to explain it explicitly.
I've been blogging for a few years myself: one post every few months. They are long pieces which I pour a ridiculous amount of effort into. And I do it for myself, even though the ostensible goal is to explain something I found interesting in my work to anyone who might be interested. And I put a lot of effort into making it accessible. The only time I've explicitly mentioned who it is for happens to be my latest and by far most popular article. However, I see that as an accident: a lot of people asked for a more nitty gritty focus. I obliged, adding a disclaimer that it was written for a different target audience than the rest. Turns out it was a better fit for my writing.

comments.author: TFNA
comments.text: 99% of open-web bloggers are going to get no significant human eyeballs on their posts regardless of whether they are willing to make overtures to their readers or not. Faced with that fact, a blogger should just write however he feels like, and then the LLM crawlers can do the business of making the facts most palatable to a human readership.

comments.text:
I have written over 200+ Twitter threads (and indexed them on a website here [0]).
If there is one thing I have learned from this experience:
It is VERY hard to predict when a piece of writing will go viral or "do numbers". You do sometimes get a sense of what people like and how to tell a good story etc but actually determining "this will be a hit!" is difficult.
Apparently, famous artists have said the same thing. e.g. Bruce Springsteen has written HUNDREDS of songs and he often says even he doesn't know why some of them become hits. Elton John apparently has a similar view.
0 -

comments.author: lbriner
comments.text:
A much more important point for respecting your readers imho when discussing something that the reader
is
interested in/needs to fix (e.g. fixing a strange bug) is to give the solution at the start and then go into the detailed explanation about how you found it.
Sometimes I am really interested in e.g. how Cloudflare found a CPU bug and the journey to get there, other times I just want to fix something and don't want to start reading an entire paragraph, "C# is a language from Microsoft designed to target the .Net framework.....", which you often see on the click-bait blogs.

comments.author: joshstrange
comments.text:
I write for myself. As a way to formulate my thoughts and record them down. If others get value from that, so be it, but once I hit publish I’ve already “succeeded”. I’ve spent considerable time writing my (few) blog posts over the years but it’s not out of some expectation of return. I don’t have ads, no subscription, no platform. Just me and my words on my own little corner of the internet.
I was doing this and thinking this way even before LLMs and they haven’t really changed the calculus for me. If anything they give me hope more people might, indirectly, benefit from what I write, potentially without even reading it. I’m ok with that.
Because again, I write for me.

comments.author: Brajeshwar

comments.author: klodolph
comments.text:
I think bloggers should mostly write how they feel like. Yes, there’s an audience, or a potential audience, but you calculate how much you want to optimize for the audience and how much to optimize for other qualities.
Maybe you are optimizing for the enjoyment of blogging. Maybe you are optimizing for getting your thoughts down in fixed form, because you think there you have something important to say. Maybe you are optimizing for blogging as a habit. It takes time to edit blog posts down and make them brief, and if you have
other shit to do
, the posts could be longer.
Next, you don't know whether a blog post will be popular / reposted / recirculated. It happens after you write it. By then, it is too late to decide whether you want to write it carefully.
Rather than assume people are not interested in my blog posts, I just believe that I don’t know which blog posts of mine people want to read, and then I’m happy when one gets higher readership.

- had to be a big country
- with spread out cities

comments.author: gumby
comments.text:
It's great that it has such a lineage and is still around, but according to its history it was a bbs / netnews login host.  World.std.com was providing internet access in 89 or 90 by log in, and of course many universities by then had hordes of people dialing up, logging in, and using the net;  A similar BBS->net hybrid was the Well.
Pobably The Little Garden (later TLGNet) in 1990 was the first ISP in the sense it's used today: there were no user hosts that you logged into and then ran programs; it literally only provided IP service and you had to have a router to connect.
We gave instructions on how to make a router with KA9Q and and an old PC, to those who needed it.
Fun trivia: the first person who managed TLG full time (before that it was just a spinoff of Cygnus, with its first POP my spare bedroom) was Tom Jennings, the author of FIDONET one of the Ur-BBS systems, and surely the biggest.
There are a lot of folks from that time on HN.
PS: the name The Little Garden came from my favorite restaurant back then, a famous hacker hangout where folks from PARC, Stanford, SRI, Sun etc would hang out.  Gosper was a regular.

comments.author: michalsustr
comments.text:
It’s a long article, and the most important idea is buried towards the end:
> That’s where I come back to the idea of mechanism design as reverse game theory. Rather than asking ourselves the rules of the game we are now playing, it calls us to ask “What game ought we to be playing?” And that question leads me imperatively to my answer: “The game of human flourishing.”
I wholeheartedly agree: we should think way harder about what we want humanity to optimize for collectively, rather than keeping it haphazard.
The current economic system is built on the idea of ‘shareholder value maximisation’, which, in a finite world, will ultimately become simply ‘value extraction’. With AI, we’ve built an automated value extractor, which can extract value even faster than was done before. Because of that, the old model can no longer work for improving human flourishing — in a finite world, it will inevitably lead to economic accumulation by few entities, throttling the economic flow.

comments.author: Animats
comments.text:
Attempts at governance are futile until we recognize that we have built a machine and set it on its course. Instead, we pretend that the market is a natural phenomenon best left alone, and we fail to hold its mechanism designers to account. We need to tear down and rebuild that machine, reprogramming it so that human flourishing, not corporate profit, becomes its goal.
This article has useful insights. It points out that capitalism is an optimization engine for something. Shareholder value and CEO compensation, mostly. It reminds us of something that many people would prefer be forgotten - capitalism operates under rules set by governments, and those shape the market. Tax law matters - what's deductible warps spending patterns. Bankruptcy law matters - who gets left holding the bag? Corporation law matters - how immune are executives from the consequences of their decisions? Labor law matters - do people go to jail for wage and hour law violations?
All of those are changeable by legislation. Most have become much more favorable to companies since 1970. That's not necessarily permanent. We had a New Deal in the 1930s, following the Gilded Age of the 1920s and the crash of 1929.
